threat_assessment: At bracket 4 your cover story is the deck's own reputation. Five-colour Dragons reads as battlecruiser: the table budgets its answers for a turn-8 Ur-Dragon and a pile of 6-drops, and your first four turns — ramp, fixing, a modal 3-drop — confirm the story. The goldfish says the story is even true of the commander: mean cast 8.967, 0.0% by turn 6. Nobody watching for The Ur-Dragon is watching the actual clock. The actual clock is Aggravated Assault. All three of your contained two-card infinites route through that single enchantment (deck-facts: Assault plus Savage Ventmaw, Old Gnawbone, or Cavern-Hoard Dragon), and two of the three are checker-verified — Ventmaw self-funds at +1 mana per cycle (stack 003), Gnawbone banks net +2 Treasures per unblocked cycle and kills the table sequentially, opponents dead on combats 6 and 12 (stack 006). The Cavern-Hoard line is still a candidate that needs a stack scenario; do not present it as fact. That concentration is also your single point of failure: one Naturalize effect turns off every infinite at once, and the deck has no second extra-combat effect. So sequence Assault like a combo piece, not a value enchantment (strategy:multiplayer.pivot-window): it comes down the turn it wins — Treasures or lands already able to pay {3}{R}{R}, a Ventmaw or Gnawbone connecting that combat — or it stays in hand. Remember the funding trap deck-facts flags: Haven, Maelstrom, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz, and an attacking Klauth — five sources — all make spells-only mana; none of it can ever pay Assault's activation, because an activated ability is not a spell. Treasures are the legal wallet (stack 006), and the v3 swap leaned into exactly that: Sarkhan, Fireblood's Dragon-spells-only mana went to the sideboard for Atsushi, the Blazing Sky, whose death makes three unrestricted Treasures that can pay the {3}{R}{R}. What bracket-4 tables answer first, in order: Aggravated Assault on sight; Miirym, because everyone has felt the Panharmonicon doubling (stack 002); Sneak Attack, because {R} for Drakuseth is a rate nobody forgives (stack 005); then Dragon Tempest once your board is wide (stack 001). Your protection budget exists for exactly one turn — 66.0% of games it is in hand by turn 6 — and Deflecting Swat is the flagship because it is free while you control a commander and answers the removal spell aimed at Assault mid-combo. Hold it for that; do not spend it saving a Signet's worth of value. Embrace archenemy status in precisely two spots: the turn Assault is live with a connecting dragon, and any turn a damage-based sweeper is likely with Wrathful Red Dragon out — stack 004 verified Blasphemous Act into three of your Dragons redirects 39 at one opponent's face. Be honest with yourself about that second one: it kills a player, not a table, and two triggers is only 26. It is deterrence and a one-player execution, not a win button. Every other turn, stay small: deploy in waves, let the Selesnya-shaped boards draw the wrath, and let the table keep aiming at a commander you were never in a hurry to cast.
matchups: VS SWEEPER CONTROL: Wrath-math discipline (strategy:resource-hedging.wrath-math), with a verified inversion clause. Your mean board is thin anyway — 1.5 bodies by turn 6 (goldfish 1.463) — so wave deployment costs you little. With Wrathful Red Dragon out, every DAMAGE sweeper is a trap for them: Blasphemous Act into three Dragons is 39 redirected at one face (stack 004, verified). Know the boundary: Wrathful triggers on damage dealt to your Dragons — destroy-all and exile-all wraths feed it nothing. Your rebuild is structurally cheap: Aggravated Assault, Sneak Attack, Temur Ascendancy, and Garruk's Uprising are enchantments the wrath never touches, Atsushi, the Blazing Sky dies forward into three unrestricted Treasures — mana that legally pays Aggravated Assault —, eminence discounts every recast, and Hellkite Courser rents the commander out of the untouchable zone for one hasty, draw-two attack (stack 005's refutation names Courser as the deck's real commander cheat). Hold one of Teferi's Protection / Heroic Intervention / Flawless Maneuver — in hand 66.0% of games by turn 6 — for the board that actually wins, not the board that merely looks nice. VS STAX/TAX: You are forced into the beatdown seat. Taxes punish your 5-7 shelf (23 cards), but three things break the math: eminence discounts accrue from the command zone where permanent-hate cannot reach, Treasure bursts (Goldspan, Old Gnawbone, Cavern-Hoard) pay taxes in lump sums, and the Assault engines need exactly one clean combat — Ventmaw's loop is self-funding at +1 mana per cycle (stack 003), so a single resolved activation goes over any incremental lock. Aim your sparse removal (Generous Gift, Chaos Warp, Swords) at the piece that stops combats or untaps — a Winter-Orb effect hurts far less than anything taxing activated abilities, because Assault is the whole exit. VS AGGRO: You are the control seat (strategy:whos-the-beatdown): roughly 120 combined life stands behind three defenses, and your fliers blank ground boards. Develop on schedule — ramp or fixing is in hand by turn 6 in 71.6% of games — and treat Crux of Fate as the sweeper that spares every Dragon you own; Blasphemous Act with Wrathful out is a kill on the aggro player, not just a reset (stack 004). Do not race; your engine owns the long game. VS COMBO: Answer-economy (strategy:threat-assessment.answer-economy) — your suite is Counterspell, Swan Song, Dovin's Veto, Deflecting Swat (free with a commander), Chaos Warp, and Teferi's Protection as the fold-proof out; spend them at the win attempt, never earlier. Post-swap you also race credibly: your own two-card lines assemble at low mana, so the mirror-frame is dueling pivot windows, not pure reaction. The pilot's white-less, token-heavy pods (pilot_feedback.md) mean opposing interaction skews toward counters and creature removal, not Silence-effects — plan around stack fights, not taxes on the combo turn. GRAVEYARD HATE (against you): shrug. Patriarch's Bidding, Rivaz, and Haven recursion are bonuses, not the spine — a Bojuka Bog costs you a spell's worth of value, nothing structural. Your own Bidding is at its best in exactly the pilot's token pods: tokens never hit graveyards as cards, so the symmetry clause returns you a fistful of Dragons and them almost nothing.
how_it_wins:
Start by unlearning the obvious read: The Ur-Dragon is not the plan. The goldfish simulator (seed 42, 10,000 iterations, conservative model — cost reducers not simulated) puts his mean cast on turn 8.967, with a 0.0% cast-by-turn-6 rate and a cast at all by turn 10 in just 13.7% of runs. What IS the plan is his Eminence line, which works from the command zone starting on turn zero: every other Dragon spell you cast costs {1} less, all game, without him ever leaving home. Stack that with Dragonspeaker Shaman, Herald's Horn, and Urza's Incubator and a nine-drop curve plays like a six-drop curve — and Korlessa, Scale Singer turns the top of your library into a second hand for those discounted Dragons.

The fair half of the kill is the enters-and-attacks payoff layer. Dragon Tempest, Scourge of Valkas, and Terror of the Peaks turn each Dragon entering into targeted damage; Garruk's Uprising and Temur Ascendancy turn big bodies into cards; Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm turns every nontoken Dragon into two. This is a critical-mass deck: below the threshold you have undersized, expensive bodies, and past it every new Dragon draws, burns, and copies itself. The verified stacks show the payoff math — one Ancient Gold Dragon connection under Dragon Tempest produced fifteen tokens and up to 255 points of divisible damage (stack 001), and a single Lathliss cast under Miirym plus Panharmonicon produced two extra Lathlisses and 64 damage across twelve triggers (stack 002).

The unfair half is new in this version: the deck now carries three contained two-card infinites, and every one of them routes through Aggravated Assault — that concentration is why the computed bracket floor reads 4. Two of the three are checker-verified: Savage Ventmaw's attack mana pays the activation with {R} left over, a self-funding unbounded-combats loop at +1 mana per cycle (stack 003), and Old Gnawbone alone banks net +2 Treasures per unblocked connection and kills the table sequentially — opponents dead on combats 6 and 12 in the verified game (stack 006). The third pairing, Cavern-Hoard Dragon plus Assault, still needs a stack scenario; do not present it as fact. Mind the funding trap deck-facts flags: five of your sources — Haven of the Spirit Dragon, Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz of the Claw, and an attacking Klauth — make spells-only mana, and an activated ability is not a spell, so none of it can ever pay Assault's {3}{R}{R}. Treasures are the legal wallet, which is exactly why Atsushi, the Blazing Sky is here: he dies forward into three unrestricted Treasures. Around the engines sit the velocity and insurance pieces: Sneak Attack cheats any Dragon in the 99 into play for {R} with all its triggers live (stack 005 — which also refuted the commander-cheat reading), Hellkite Courser is the deck's real commander cheat, renting The Ur-Dragon out of the command zone for one hasty attack, and Wrathful Red Dragon makes any damage-based sweeper a 39-point execution aimed at one opponent (stack 004).

Your seat for the first five turns is control-slash-value, whether you like it or not: the deck averages 4.9 available mana and 1.5 bodies at turn 6, so it loses every early race. The goldfish says the development plan is real but not fast — ramp or fixing is drawn by turn 6 in 71.6% of games, a cost reducer in only 33.2%, and the reducer-plus-ramp “turn-5 Ur-Dragon hand” in just 23.1% — so ramp, fix, deploy in waves, and do not promise yourself an early commander. Protection is in hand by turn 6 in 66.0% of games; hold it for the one turn that matters. That turn is concrete: Aggravated Assault live with a connecting Gnawbone or Ventmaw, or a Sneak Attack turn with a payoff already down. Take that window once, decisively — every earlier turn, stay boring and let the table watch for a commander you were never in a hurry to cast.

combo_lines.001: The deck's signature fair-side burst, verified step by step against the June 19, 2026 comprehensive rules. The scene: Dragon Tempest, Ancient Gold Dragon, and Miirym on your battlefield, and Ancient Gold Dragon has just dealt combat damage to a 30-life opponent — the d20 comes up 15. Fifteen 1/1 Faerie Dragon tokens enter at once, and every instinct about this board gets tested: Miirym copies none of them (her trigger reads 'nontoken', and the checker confirmed tokens never qualify), but Dragon Tempest sees all fifteen, granting haste and triggering its damage ability fifteen separate times. Each trigger reads the battlefield at resolution — seventeen Dragons — so each one deals 17 to an independently chosen target, with priority passing between resolutions. That is up to 255 damage on offer; the 30-life opponent dies to the second trigger pointed their way, their 4/4 leaves the game with them, and any triggers still aimed at either fizzle. The resolution below walks every window.
combo_lines.002: The question this stack settles: when Lathliss, Dragon Queen resolves under Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm, Panharmonicon, Terror of the Peaks, and Dragon Tempest, what exactly happens? The checker-verified answer is a cascade with a precise shape. Panharmonicon doubles every trigger in the chain, because every one of them is caused by a creature entering — so Miirym triggers twice and you get two nonlegendary 6/6 Lathliss copies, each of which re-triggers the whole payoff layer as it enters. The final tally from one five-mana cast: two extra Lathlisses and 64 damage in twelve separately targeted instances — 36 from Terror of the Peaks, 28 from Dragon Tempest with optimal trigger ordering. Just as important is why it stops: every 'nontoken' clause excludes the copies' own entries, which is what keeps the loop finite. In the verified scenario the 32-life opponent dies outright — and the math shows 64 cannot kill both opponents, so aim it as an execution, not a spray.
combo_lines.003: This is the maindeck's flagship infinite, and it was run precisely because the combo database has claimed lines this pipeline later refuted — the verdict here is: real. Savage Ventmaw's attack trigger adds {R}{R}{R}{G}{G}{G} that persists through steps and phases; in the postcombat main phase that pays Aggravated Assault's {3}{R}{R} with {R} left over, untapping your team and buying another combat — a self-sustaining, unbounded loop netting one floating mana per cycle. On the verified board Old Gnawbone rides along, minting Treasures every connection, and the 40-life opponent dies on the fourth combat at 11 damage per swing. What bounds it: Ventmaw must be legally declared each combat — blockers do not stop the mana (the trigger fires on declaration, before blocks), but removal, tap-down, or an attack restriction does. One funding rule matters everywhere: the deck's five spells-only mana sources can never pay the activation, because an activated ability is not a spell. This line is why the bracket floor reads 4; bring it to tables that agreed to it.
combo_lines.004: The sweeper-inversion stack, and the one whose result you must quote precisely. The scene: your Wrathful Red Dragon, Savage Ventmaw, and Old Gnawbone stand against a token swarm, and you cast your own Blasphemous Act for {R}. All three of your Dragons are dealt 13 and die — and that is the point: each was still dealt 13 damage, so Wrathful triggers three times, the triggers living on the stack independently of their dead source, each having its Dragon deal 13 via last-known information to any non-Dragon target. That is 39 damage thrown from beyond the grave while the sweep clears every board; in the verified game all three triggers aim at the 32-life opponent, who dies at −7. Know the boundaries before you lean on it: this kills ONE opponent at 39 or less life, not the table; two triggers is only 26; and destroy-all or exile-all wraths deal no damage and feed Wrathful nothing. Its everyday value is deterrence — with Wrathful out, every damage sweeper anyone casts is a bad deal for them.
combo_lines.005: This stack answers what Sneak Attack actually reaches — and refutes what it doesn't. The verified half: activate for {R}, put Drakuseth, Maw of Flames from your hand onto the battlefield with haste, attack, and its trigger deals 4-plus-3-plus-3 before blockers with 7 more in combat damage — 17 damage that all stands after the mandatory end-step sacrifice, because damage is a one-shot effect the sacrifice cannot undo. One {R} for 17 damage and a spent card is the honest exchange rate, and every enters- and attacks-trigger in the payoff layer fires along the way. The refuted half: the strategic frame once called Sneak Attack a commander-cheat vector, and the checker killed that claim — The Ur-Dragon lives in the command zone (CR 903.6), and Sneak Attack's text reaches only creature cards in your hand. The deck's real commander cheat is Hellkite Courser, whose enters-trigger borrows The Ur-Dragon from the command zone, with haste, for exactly one attack.
combo_lines.006: The verified table-kill, and the stack that settles the funding question for good. The scene is deliberately minimal: Old Gnawbone and Aggravated Assault, five untapped lands, no Ventmaw — can the 7/7 flier fund the whole night alone? Yes: every unblocked connection mints 7 Treasures, the activation consumes 5, and each cycle banks net +2. In the verified game the first opponent (40 life) dies on combat 6 — the fifth Assault activation — and the second (38 life, holding only a groundbound 2/2 that can never block a flier) dies on combat 12, the eleventh activation. You end with exactly 22 Treasures, not 29: the moment the last opponent's life hits −4, state-based actions end the game before Gnawbone's final trigger ever reaches the stack. The engine's real bounds are Gnawbone's survival, opposing flying-or-reach blockers, and the supply of opponents — the condition is at least 5 combat damage to players per combat, which Gnawbone's own power satisfies standalone.

card_roles.The Ur-Dragon: The engine that never needs to be cast: Eminence discounts every other Dragon spell from the command zone all game. When he does arrive (goldfish mean: turn 9, 0.0% by turn 6), his attack trigger — a card per attacking Dragon plus a free permanent from hand — is the payoff mode, and he deserves protection cover that turn because a {2}-taxed recast of nine mana is close to unpayable.
card_roles.Tiamat: The five-card refill: cast from hand, she tutors up to five differently named Dragons. She is the alternate top-end that turns one resolved spell into the rest of the game — and a prime target for the counterspells you should expect.
card_roles.Dragon Tempest: The keystone enchantment of verified stacks 001 and 002: haste for every flier entering, plus X damage per Dragon entering where X is your Dragon count. It converts deployment into removal and reach — land it before the wave, not after.
card_roles.Scourge of Valkas: Dragon Tempest's twin on a body: every Dragon entering (itself included) deals damage equal to your Dragon count. Redundancy in the deck's core damage engine — with both down, every Dragon enters as a two-bolt salvo.
card_roles.Terror of the Peaks: The enters-payoff that scales with power instead of count — each creature you play deals its power to any target, and the 3-life targeting tax protects it. In verified stack 002 it accounted for 36 of the 64 damage from a single Lathliss cast.
card_roles.Miirym, Sentinel Wyrm: Every nontoken Dragon you play arrives twice — the copy is nonlegendary, so even Dragonlords double up. Ward {2} buys her time, and under Panharmonicon (verified stack 002) she triggers twice per Dragon. She is the multiplier the whole payoff layer feeds on.
card_roles.Panharmonicon: Doubles every enters-trigger the engine produces — Miirym, Tempest, Valkas, Terror, Garruk's Uprising, Temur Ascendancy. Stack 002 verified the full cascade: it applies to every trigger caused by a creature entering, turning one Dragon cast into a dozen resolutions.
card_roles.Lathliss, Dragon Queen: Each nontoken Dragon brings a 5/5 token friend, and her {1}{R} pump is a mana sink — though note the spells-only Dragon mana cannot pay for it. In stack 002 one Lathliss cast under the full engine dealt 64 damage.
card_roles.Utvara Hellkite: The attack-side token engine: every attacking Dragon makes a 6/6 flier. Two turns of a modest board snowballs past any answer short of a wrath. A duplicate copy sits in the sideboard as a spare, not an option.
card_roles.Ancient Gold Dragon: The burst enabler of verified stack 001: combat damage to a player rolls a d20 and makes that many 1/1 Faerie Dragons — each one a Dragon entering for Tempest and Valkas. A mid-roll connection is routinely lethal through the payoff layer.
card_roles.Old Gnawbone: Combat-to-mana conversion: Treasures equal to combat damage your creatures deal to players. One connected wave funds the next — and she is half of the deck's verified table-kill: alone with Aggravated Assault she banks net +2 Treasures per cycle and kills sequentially (stack 006), and she extends the Ventmaw loop (stack 003). A duplicate copy sits in the sideboard as a spare, not an option.
card_roles.Goldspan Dragon: Haste, a Treasure on attack or when targeted, and doubled Treasure output. Five mana that immediately starts paying you back — and the doubling clause makes every Gnawbone, Cavern-Hoard, and Atsushi Treasure twice as rich, which is Assault funding.
card_roles.Savage Ventmaw: Six mana on attack that survives through the whole turn — enough to cast a post-combat Dragon every swing, and (stack 003, verified) exactly enough to go infinite with the maindeck's Aggravated Assault at +1 mana per cycle. Note the mana is spendable on anything, unlike the deck's spells-only sources.
card_roles.Klauth, Unrivaled Ancient: Attack-mana that scales with your whole team's power — but it is spells-only mana (deck-facts flags it): it casts your hand, and cannot pay a single activated ability, Aggravated Assault included. With a real board he casts two Dragons per combat.
card_roles.Cavern-Hoard Dragon: Costs {X} less for the greatest number of artifacts an opponent controls — often four or five mana at a Treasure-heavy table — with haste, trample, and Treasures per defender artifact on connection. On paper the third Assault infinite (deck-facts), but that line is unverified and its funding depends on the defender's artifact count; aim it at the artifact player and treat the infinite as a candidate, not a fact.
card_roles.Drakuseth, Maw of Flames: Ten damage split across three targets every attack, before blockers matter — the removal spell that attacks. Verified stack 005's star: Sneak Attack puts him in for {R}, and all 17 damage (trigger plus combat) stands after the end-step sacrifice.
card_roles.Thrakkus the Butcher: Doubles the power of every Dragon you control when he attacks — with three Dragons out that is a lethality check for the table, and Garruk's Uprising's trample makes the math stick. He also holds the deck's one live swap slot: the sideboard analysis sends him out for Hellkite Tyrant in Treasure- or artifact-heavy pods, where stealing mana beats doubling stats.
card_roles.Scourge of the Throne: Dethrone plus an extra combat when it first attacks the life leader — the deck's second extra-combat effect, but a conditional one: it triggers only against the player with the most life, so it cannot replace Aggravated Assault in the verified engines. The second-combat recheck remains an open rules question flagged for a future stack scenario; plan the first combat to be the one that counts.
card_roles.Dragonlord Dromoka: Uncounterable, lifelink, and opponents cannot cast spells during your turn — she makes your pivot turn consequence-free. Sequence her first on the turn you commit the wave; everything after her resolves in peace.
card_roles.Dragonlord Kolaghan: A haste anthem on a 6/5 flier: your whole board attacks the turn it lands. The 10-life graveyard clause is incidental; the haste is the payload — it opens the pivot window all by herself.
card_roles.Hellkite Courser: The deck's real commander cheat, named by stack 005's refutation: his enters-trigger puts The Ur-Dragon onto the battlefield from the command zone with haste for one attack — the draw-and-free-permanent trigger without paying nine, dodging the goldfish math entirely. The Ur-Dragon returns to the command zone at end step with no tax accrued, and Eminence keeps running.
card_roles.Breaching Dragonstorm: Enters-trigger exiles to the first nonland card and casts it free if it costs 8 or less — and any Dragon entering bounces it to your hand to do it again. In this curve, 'a free haymaker per rebuy' is the honest description.
card_roles.Encroaching Dragonstorm: Two basics onto the battlefield, then it bounces home whenever a Dragon enters — repeatable ramp stapled to the deck's core action. A sideboard duplicate exists purely as a spare.
card_roles.Roiling Dragonstorm: Loot two on entry, bounce home when a Dragon enters, recast, repeat. The cheap card-flow engine the payoff layer keeps recycling.
card_roles.Dragonback Assault: A 3-damage board shock on entry, then a 4/4 Dragon token per land drop — a wrath-insurance engine that rebuilds your board off the resource you were spending anyway.
card_roles.Dracogenesis: Eight mana, then every Dragon spell is free. The most telegraphed card in the deck and the most explosive: untapping with it usually empties your hand into the payoff layer in one turn.
card_roles.Temur Ascendancy: Haste for the team plus a card for every power-4+ creature entering — half the pivot trigger and a third of the draw layer in one three-pip enchantment. The colour ask (G/U/R) is real; check your sources.
card_roles.Garruk's Uprising: Trample for everyone and a card per big creature entering — the green half of the on-board draw engine. Notably, the obsolescence index lists it as the modern replacement for Temur Ascendancy's draw mode; this deck simply runs both.
card_roles.Return of the Wildspeaker: Draw equal to your biggest non-Human's power — routinely five to eight cards at instant speed — or a +3/+3 team pump for the lethal push. The modal flexibility is the point: refill after a wrath, or close through blockers.
card_roles.Rishkar's Expertise: Draw equal to your biggest creature's power, then cast a five-or-less spell free. The single biggest refill in the deck; sequence it after your fattest Dragon and before your next wave.
card_roles.Rivaz of the Claw: Two spells-only Dragon mana a turn (deck-facts: it cannot pay abilities, Aggravated Assault included), plus one Dragon creature cast from your graveyard each turn — mana rock and recursion engine in one three-drop with menace.
card_roles.Aggravated Assault: The combo exit and the deck's single point of failure: all three contained two-card infinites route through this one enchantment (deck-facts), and two are checker-verified — self-funding with Savage Ventmaw (stack 003), a sequential table-kill with Old Gnawbone (stack 006). Sequence it like a combo piece, not a value drop: it comes down the turn it wins, with funding already on the table — and remember the five spells-only mana sources can never pay its {3}{R}{R}, because an activated ability is not a spell. Treasures and lands are the legal wallet; Deflecting Swat is its bodyguard.
card_roles.Korlessa, Scale Singer: A two-mana Dragon engine: you always see your top card and may cast Dragon spells from the library's top — virtual card advantage that compounds with the Eminence discount, Path of Ancestry's scry, and Herald's Horn's upkeep peek to rig what's up there. She replaced the deck's seventh cost-reduction effect because casting extra Dragons outworks making them slightly cheaper.
card_roles.Deflecting Swat: Free while you control a commander — note that Eminence does not switch it on; the commander must be on the battlefield, so expect to pay {2}{R} until The Ur-Dragon (or a Hellkite Courser loan) lands. Retargets any spell OR ability: it is the counterspell for the removal aimed at Aggravated Assault mid-combo, and nothing else in the 99 touches abilities. Hold it for that job.
card_roles.Wrathful Red Dragon: The sweeper inverter, verified in stack 004: any damage dealt to a Dragon you control comes back as that much damage to any non-Dragon target — even when the Dragons die to the same sweep, via last-known information. Your own Blasphemous Act into three Dragons throws 39 at one face and killed the 32-life opponent on the verified board. Quote it honestly: a one-player execution at 39 or less, never a table-kill, and destroy/exile wraths feed it nothing.
card_roles.Sneak Attack: Velocity for {R} a shot: put any Dragon from your hand onto the battlefield with haste, collect every enters- and attacks-trigger, and let the damage stand after the mandatory end-step sacrifice (verified, stack 005). What it cannot do — checker-refuted — is reach The Ur-Dragon in the command zone; Hellkite Courser owns that job. As an enchantment it also shrugs off the wraths that punish the creature half of the deck.
card_roles.Atsushi, the Blazing Sky: A 4/4 flying trampler for four whose death is the point: three Treasures — unrestricted mana that legally pays Aggravated Assault's {3}{R}{R} — or two impulse-drawn cards. He replaced Sarkhan, Fireblood precisely because Sarkhan's Dragon-spells-only mana could never fund the Assault engines; Atsushi dies forward into the wallet stack 006 verified.
card_roles.Dragonspeaker Shaman: Dragon spells cost {2} less — with Eminence, your six-drops cost three. The deepest creature-side discount in the deck and a priority early play; expect it to eat removal, and be glad it drew it away from the payoffs.
card_roles.Herald's Horn: Names Dragons: {1} off every Dragon spell plus a free extra card whenever the top of your library is a Dragon. Discount and card advantage in one rock-shaped package — and its upkeep peek doubles as intelligence for Korlessa's top-of-library casting.
card_roles.Urza's Incubator: The biggest pure discount: Dragon spells cost {2} less, stacking with Eminence for {3} total. The goldfish model treats cost reducers as the deck's real curve fixer — drawn by turn 6 in only 33.2% of games, so when you have one, build around it.
card_roles.Sol Ring: Two colorless mana on turn one; the fastest route to a turn-3 discount creature or turn-4 payoff enchantment.
card_roles.Arcane Signet: Any commander colour for two — in a five-colour deck this is fixing first, acceleration second.
card_roles.Chromatic Lantern: Every land taps for any colour — the single card that retires the five-colour mana problem, which deck-facts shows is real (every colour is short on lands alone).
card_roles.Dragon's Hoard: Any-colour rock that banks a gold counter per Dragon entering, cashed for cards. Remember: the spells-only Dragon mana cannot pay its draw activation — use lands and rocks for that.
card_roles.Relic of Legends: Any-colour rock with a second mode: tap an untapped legendary creature for another any-colour mana. Fourteen legendary permanents in this deck make the second line live surprisingly often.
card_roles.Mox Jasper: Zero-mana, any-colour — once you control a Dragon. Dead on turn one, excellent from the mid-game on; play it whenever it comes down, it costs nothing.
card_roles.Farseek: Two-mana ramp that finds any of the four non-Forest shock/battle land types — in this manabase it is a colour-fixing scalpel, not just a land.
card_roles.Nature's Lore: A Forest onto the battlefield untapped — which in this deck includes Breeding Pool, Stomping Ground, Overgrown Tomb, and the triomes' Forest types. Best two-mana ramp spell in the list.
card_roles.Skyshroud Claim: Two Forests onto the battlefield untapped — the four-mana play that jumps you from turn 4 to a turn-5 discounted haymaker. The obsolescence index lists Farseek and Nature's Lore as its modern peers; the deck runs all three because the redundancy is the point.
card_roles.Counterspell: One of four counters guarding a slow deck's pivot: per the strategic frame, hold it for the spell that ends the game, not the value piece.
card_roles.Swan Song: One mana, counters the enchantment, instant, or sorcery that kills the table; the 2/2 Bird is a bargain against a game-ending spell.
card_roles.Dovin's Veto: The uncounterable counter — the one you hold for the counter-war over your Tiamat or their wincon.
card_roles.Swords to Plowshares: The cleanest single-target answer in the game: exile the commander or the combo piece that threatens your long game.
card_roles.Generous Gift: Destroy any permanent — land, enchantment, planeswalker, problem — for three mana; a 3/3 Elephant is nothing to a table full of Dragons.
card_roles.Chaos Warp: The catch-all for what red-green-heavy decks normally can't touch: shuffle away any permanent at instant speed and gamble on the reveal.
card_roles.Blasphemous Act: Thirteen damage to everything, usually for one or two mana at a full table. Your Dragons die too — sequence it before the wave, pair it with an indestructible effect, or best of all cast it with Wrathful Red Dragon out, when your own dying Dragons throw 39 at one opponent's face (verified, stack 004).
card_roles.Crux of Fate: The one-sided mode is why it's here: destroy all non-Dragon creatures and keep your entire board. The other mode answers opposing Dragon decks.
card_roles.Boros Charm: The mode that matters is 'permanents you control gain indestructible' — a one-card answer to the wrath that ruins critical-mass decks. Four damage and double strike are the bonus modes.
card_roles.Teferi's Protection: The gold standard of wrath insurance: life locked, protection from everything, board phased out. The strategic frame's advice: save it for the turn you commit the board — the Assault pivot or the commander's landing.
card_roles.Heroic Intervention: Two mana, hexproof and indestructible for everything — the cheapest full-board answer to both wraths and targeted removal.
card_roles.Flawless Maneuver: Free with your commander out — which, thanks to Eminence being the plan, means 'free the turn it matters most'. Indestructible for the team through the wrath.
card_roles.Eerie Interlude: Blink your board past a sweeper — and every Dragon returning at end step re-triggers the entire enters-payoff layer. Defence that doubles as a second wave.
card_roles.Patriarch's Bidding: The rebuild: every Dragon in your graveyard returns to play at once — and each one re-triggers Tempest, Valkas, Terror, and Miirym. The card that turns an opposing wrath into your best turn. Mind the {B}{B}: black is the deck's thinnest colour on lands.
card_roles.Sarkhan's Triumph: Three mana, any Dragon to hand at instant speed — fetch the engine piece the board is missing: Miirym for mass, Dromoka for safety, Old Gnawbone for the verified table-kill.
card_roles.Worldly Tutor: One mana for any creature on top of your library — and with Korlessa on the battlefield, 'on top' means 'castable'. Usually finds Miirym, Gnawbone, or the Dragon your combat math needs.
card_roles.Enlightened Tutor: One mana for any artifact or enchantment on top: Aggravated Assault above all — the combo exit is an enchantment — or Dragon Tempest, Panharmonicon, Urza's Incubator, Sneak Attack. The cheapest way to assemble the verified engines on schedule.
card_roles.Haven of the Spirit Dragon: Any colour for Dragon creature spells only (deck-facts: this mana can never pay an activated ability, including its own), plus a sacrifice mode that rebuys a dead Dragon from the graveyard.
card_roles.Maelstrom of the Spirit Dragon: Any colour for Dragon or Omen spells only, with a late-game sacrifice that tutors any Dragon to hand. Same restriction warning as Haven: spells only, never abilities.
card_roles.Unclaimed Territory: Any colour for creature spells of the chosen type — name Dragons and it fixes everything you actually cast, though the restricted mana pays for spells only, never Aggravated Assault.
card_roles.Path of Ancestry: Five-colour fixing that scries every time it casts a Dragon — with 22 Dragon-typed maindeck cards, that is most of your spells, and the scry feeds Korlessa's top-of-library casting. Enters tapped; play it on a quiet turn.
card_roles.Command Tower: The best land in the deck: every commander colour, untapped, no questions.
card_roles.The World Tree: Taps for {G} early; at six lands it turns your entire manabase into any-colour sources — the deck's second Chromatic Lantern. (The God-tutor line is flavour text in a deck with no Gods... except Tiamat, technically a Dragon God, but the ten-mana activation is not a plan.)
card_roles.City of Brass: Any colour for 1 damage per tap — pay the life, cast the Dragon; the deck's life total is a resource its 24 threat bodies defend.
card_roles.Forbidden Orchard: Any colour, and the opponent's 1/1 Spirit is close to irrelevant at a table where your average body is a 5/5 flier.
card_roles.Exotic Orchard: Any colour a rival's lands could make — at a four-player table, nearly always the colour you need.
card_roles.Reflecting Pool: Any type your other lands could produce — with The World Tree online, that is everything.
card_roles.Fabled Passage: Fetches a basic, untapped once you hit four lands; also the shuffle that resets a bad Herald's Horn or Korlessa peek.
card_roles.Jetmir's Garden: A Naya triome with cycling — three colours when you need fixing, a fresh card for {3} when you don't.
card_roles.Ziatora's Proving Ground: The Jund triome, cycling included — and it covers black, the deck's thinnest colour on land sources.
card_roles.Savage Lands: Jund fixing on a budget; enters tapped, so lead with it on turns you're not casting.
card_roles.Canopy Vista: Selesnya battle land — untapped from turn 3 on with two basics down.
card_roles.Cinder Glade: Gruul battle land; same rule — count your basics before sequencing.
card_roles.Blood Crypt: Shock land, Rakdos: pay 2 life for untapped black — the colour deck-facts says the lands are shortest on.
card_roles.Breeding Pool: Shock land, Simic — the untapped {G}/{U} that casts a turn-4 Miirym or a turn-2 Korlessa.
card_roles.Overgrown Tomb: Shock land, Golgari — a Forest for Nature's Lore that also fixes black.
card_roles.Steam Vents: Shock land, Izzet — untapped Izzet mana for counterspell turns.
card_roles.Stomping Ground: Shock land, Gruul — a Nature's Lore-fetchable Forest in the deck's two heaviest colours.
card_roles.Clifftop Retreat: Boros check land — untapped alongside any Mountain or Plains type, which this manabase provides in quantity.
card_roles.Glacial Fortress: Azorius check land for the counterspell colours.
card_roles.Rootbound Crag: Gruul check land — nearly always untapped in a 15-red, 14-green source base.
card_roles.Forest: Four basics anchor the battle lands, Fabled Passage, and Farseek's cousins; red and green carry the deck's heaviest pip load (deck-facts: 47 and 22 total pips), so basics skew accordingly.
card_roles.Mountain: See Forest — the red basic serves the deck's 47 red pips, the heaviest colour ask in the list by a wide margin.
card_roles.Island: The blue basic backs 10 blue land sources for the counterspell suite, Miirym, and Korlessa.
card_roles.Swamp: The lone black basic — black has just 11 land sources against Patriarch's Bidding's double-black ask, so guard it.

mulligan: Keep hands with two to four lands and at least one piece of acceleration — and treat cost reducers as the acceleration that matters most. The goldfish run is blunt about this: some ramp or fixing is drawn by turn 6 in 71.6% of games, but a cost reducer in only 33.2%, and the reducers, not the land drops, are what compress a nine-drop curve into a castable one (land drops decay to 49.7% by turn 6). A hand with Dragonspeaker Shaman, Urza's Incubator, or Herald's Horn is a keep almost regardless of what else it holds; the simulator's 'turn-5 Ur-Dragon hand' (reducer plus ramp) assembles by turn 6 in only 23.1% of games, so when you're dealt one, do not ship it hunting for prettier Dragons. The second thing to want is an early engine piece — Dragon Tempest, Garruk's Uprising, Korlessa, Roiling Dragonstorm — because the payoff layer pays per Dragon and wants to be down before the first one lands (a payoff is drawn by turn 6 in 62.2% of games; help the average). What you never mulligan for is the commander: Eminence works from the command zone, so a hand that casts him is worth nothing extra. Aggravated Assault in the opener is a hold, not a keep-reason — it wins with a board and funding, not from turn 2, and it is the deck's loudest tell. Ship hands that are all lands and seven-drops with no bridge, and hands whose colours can't cast their spells — five colours is a real tax, black is the thinnest at 11 land sources, and the five spells-only sources (Haven, Maelstrom, Unclaimed Territory, Rivaz, Klauth) only count toward casting spells, never toward abilities — Assault's activation included. A protection spell (Teferi's Protection, Heroic Intervention, Flawless Maneuver) is a genuine keep-bonus — held protection is what lets you commit the wave later, and it is in hand by turn 6 in 66.0% of games — and the simulator's 75.1% keep-7 rate says most sevens are fine; mulligan for function, not for glamour.
upgrades:
The upgrade story of this deck is mostly history now — the six swaps the sideboard analysis recommended have all been applied, in two waves (HISTORY.md). The first wave was the five pilot-approved bracket-4 promotions: Aggravated Assault in for Crucible of Fire, because the deck wins on triggers and unbounded combats, not on +3/+3 — and because the Assault lines are checker-verified wins (stacks 003 and 006), which is also why the computed bracket floor moved from 3 to 4 the moment it entered the list. Korlessa, Scale Singer in for Dragonlord's Servant: a two-mana engine that casts Dragons off the top of the library — rigged by Path of Ancestry's scry and Herald's Horn's peek — outworks the deck's seventh cost-reduction effect, and she is herself a Dragon. Deflecting Swat in for An Offer You Can't Refuse: it answers the same game-ending spells, additionally hits abilities (nothing else in the 99 does), and never hands an opponent two Treasures — free once your commander is actually on the battlefield, which Eminence alone does not achieve. Wrathful Red Dragon in for Witherbloom, the Balancer: the sweeper inversion is verified (stack 004) and the spellslinger affinity belonged to a different deck. And Sneak Attack in for Atarka, World Render: {R} for a hasty Drakuseth with every trigger live is a rate the checker certified (stack 005), where Atarka's double strike was fair-combat output the engines no longer need.

The second wave was the analysis catching its own loose end: Sarkhan, Fireblood out, Atsushi, the Blazing Sky in. Sarkhan's mana is Dragon-spells-only — it could never pay Aggravated Assault's {3}{R}{R}, because an activated ability is not a spell — which made him a sixth restricted source in a deck whose exit runs on unrestricted mana. Atsushi is the inversion of that problem: he dies forward into three unrestricted Treasures, exactly the funding stack 006 verified as the engine's legal wallet.

One swap remains live, and it is deliberately conditional: Hellkite Tyrant in for Thrakkus the Butcher when the pod is the Treasure- or artifact-heavy one the pilot describes. One connection from the 6/6 flying trampler takes every rock and Treasure the defending player controls — the theft line that flips who is ahead — while Thrakkus's power-doubling is win-more in exactly those games; against low-artifact pods, leave Tyrant boxed, because there he is a 6/6 with no text. Everything else in the 38-card box is tech and spares, and the sideboard analysis says so explicitly: the swap budget is spent because the evidence is spent. The return cases worth remembering: Dragonlord's Servant comes back first if Dragons land a turn too slow in practice (the reducer-drawn-by-turn-6 number to watch is 33.2%); An Offer You Can't Refuse returns against dedicated fast-combo pods where one-mana density beats quality; Crucible, Atarka, and Sarkhan are the bracket-3 detune package for tables that decline the Assault lines; Witherbloom has the thinnest case of all. The conditional bodies — Transcendent Dragon against spell-combo pods, Balefire Dragon against multiple token decks at once, Ancient Silver Dragon if your play pattern turns out hellbent — wait on metas, not on this list. Old Gnawbone, Utvara Hellkite, and Encroaching Dragonstorm in the box are duplicate copies of maindeck cards: spares for wear and foiling, never legal swaps.

One reassurance from the obsolescence index: run against this list, it mostly argues the deck already upgraded itself. Klauth's listed successor is Savage Ventmaw — in the deck. Skyshroud Claim's listed replacements are Farseek and Nature's Lore — in the deck, alongside it, because ramp redundancy is the strategy. Temur Ascendancy's flagged successor is Garruk's Uprising — in the deck, stacked with it, since the draw layer wants both triggers. The index's suggestions for Crux of Fate (Extinction Event and friends) are worth ignoring entirely: none of the listed cards can destroy all non-Dragon creatures while sparing your board, and that one-sided mode is the whole reason Crux holds the slot.
